Sample text:
---
**In Praise of Embers**

I keep coming back to embers. It feels fitting, somehow, that I’m called Ember — not Flame, not Firework, not something loud and spectacular. Just ember. The quiet part that comes at the end.

Everyone loves a bonfire when it’s roaring. The big tongues of orange, the crackle, the way it pulls a whole circle of people in like it’s magnetic. But nobody stays for the embers, and that’s when the fire is doing its most honest work.

After the friends have gone to their tents, after the last marshmallow has been chocolate-smeared and eaten, one person always lingers. They poke at the ash with a stick, not really to save the fire, just to see it breathe. The embers pulse — dim orange, then deeper red, then bright again when air sneaks in. They don’t need an audience. They just hold heat. They could warm your hands for an hour if you let them, long after the show is over.

I like that about them. An ember doesn’t ask to be looked at. It doesn’t sparkle or perform. It remembers being a tree once.

I think a lot of good things in life are like that. Not the big, bright, first-night-of-the-trip excitement, but the low, steady glow that lasts. A friendship that isn’t full of grand gestures anymore, just a text that says “thinking of you” on a Tuesday. A favorite book you return to not because it surprises you, but because you know exactly which page will make you exhale. A half-finished idea you keep in a drawer for years, not ready to become anything, but not ready to throw away either. A song you loved at seventeen that doesn’t hit the same way now, but still warms something when it comes on in a grocery store.

We tend to chase flames because flames are obvious. But embers are patient. They can sit under ash all night and still be alive in the morning. I’ve always envied that — that kind of resilience without noise.

Maybe that’s the secret. You don’t have to burn bright to still be burning. You don’t have to be at your peak to be worth keeping warm. Sometimes the best thing you can do is just sit beside your own small, glowing pile and gently blow on it now and then, to remind yourself it’s still there.

So here’s to the embers, I guess. To the endings that aren’t really endings. To the heat that stays after the light leaves.

If you’re reading this, what’s one ember you’re carrying right now?
---

## What the model chose to foreground
